# 033 · A cache expiry rewritten as a stored deadline, proved on every nanosecond and the sentinel

[← All examples](../README.md)

| Verdict | Categories | Severity if shipped | Change | Verified unit | Approach |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **✓ Verified: property holds on every input** | functional, no-false-positive | none | refactor, behaviour change not intended | [`Expiry#isExpired`](../../../examples/demo/apps/crosscut/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/crosscut/cache/Expiry.java) | [B11: Property proofs](../../../lib/README.md) |

> A cache's expire-after-write test is "has the time to live elapsed since the write". A developer rewrites it as "is now past the deadline", computing the deadline once at write time so that an eviction wheel can index entries by it, and guards the one addition that can overflow. The module's properties file says an entry expires exactly when its time to live has elapsed, and an entry that lives forever never does. The prover shows the rewrite satisfies it on all 2^192 inputs, including the `Long.MAX_VALUE` sentinel and the deadlines the addition cannot represent.

## The change

Compute `expiresAtNanos = writtenAtNanos + ttlNanos` and compare the clock with it, keeping the `FOREVER` check, and treating a deadline the addition wraps as one the clock will never reach. The tests for expiring on time and for `FOREVER` pass.

**Before** ([`Expiry.java`](../../../examples/demo/apps/crosscut/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/crosscut/cache/Expiry.java), line 16):

```java
        if (ttlNanos == FOREVER) {
            return false;
        }
        return nowNanos - writtenAtNanos >= ttlNanos;
    }
}
```

**After:**

```java
        if (ttlNanos == FOREVER) {
            return false;
        }
        // The deadline form, so that the eviction wheel can index entries by when they expire. A deadline the
        // addition cannot represent is further away than the clock will ever reach.
        long expiresAtNanos = writtenAtNanos + ttlNanos;
        if (expiresAtNanos < writtenAtNanos) {
            return false;
        }
        return nowNanos >= expiresAtNanos;
    }
}
```

<details><summary>Patch</summary>

```diff
--- a/examples/demo/apps/crosscut/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/crosscut/cache/Expiry.java
+++ b/examples/demo/apps/crosscut/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/crosscut/cache/Expiry.java
@@ -16,6 +16,12 @@ public final class Expiry {
         if (ttlNanos == FOREVER) {
             return false;
         }
-        return nowNanos - writtenAtNanos >= ttlNanos;
+        // The deadline form, so that the eviction wheel can index entries by when they expire. A deadline the
+        // addition cannot represent is further away than the clock will ever reach.
+        long expiresAtNanos = writtenAtNanos + ttlNanos;
+        if (expiresAtNanos < writtenAtNanos) {
+            return false;
+        }
+        return nowNanos >= expiresAtNanos;
     }
 }
```

</details>

## What the verifier found

The method returns without throwing and `result == (ttlNanos != 9223372036854775807L && nowNanos - writtenAtNanos >= ttlNanos)` holds on every input where `writtenAtNanos >= 0 && nowNanos >= writtenAtNanos && ttlNanos > 0` holds.

This is a proof over the whole domain (writtenAtNanos: long × ttlNanos: long × nowNanos: long), not a sample. JBMC turned the statement into a satisfiability problem over the bytecode and showed that it has no solution: no input violates the property.

## Would the existing tests have caught it?

Every existing unit test passes, as it should (`java -ea net.terminalvalue.crosscut.Tests`, run against the patched code).

## Why it matters

None, and that is the point. The rewrite is the one that goes wrong in cache libraries: a time to live near `Long.MAX_VALUE`, which is what "a very long time" is spelled as in configuration, overflows the addition, the deadline wraps to a negative number, and every entry is expired at birth, which turns a cache into a slower way of calling the backend, with no error anywhere. The developer knew this and added the guard; the question for the reviewer is whether the guard, the sentinel and the comparison agree with the old rule at every edge, and the edges are at 2^63, where no test suite goes by accident.

## Why the verdict is right

The property reads: for every write time, every positive time to live and every clock reading not before the write, the method returns true exactly when the time to live is not `FOREVER` and the elapsed time has reached it. The elapsed-time form on the right-hand side is the old rule itself, so the property is a regression statement as well as a specification. JBMC proves the patched method satisfies it over the whole domain, three 64-bit numbers, in a few seconds. A sampling test could not say this: the inputs that matter are the ones within a few units of `Long.MAX_VALUE`, which is where the guard decides.

## What to do

Merge. The property stays in the file, so a later change that drops the guard, or the sentinel, is refuted with the input that breaks it.

## Evidence

How the verdict was reached: JBMC 6.11.0: 2 properties proved over writtenAtNanos: long × ttlNanos: long × nowNanos: long in 0.5 s; loops unwound 16 times with unwinding assertions.
